newsitem.title: USA: Ill. agency delays final action on Allstate deal.
newsitem.headline: Ill. agency delays final action on Allstate deal.

text.p: Illinois Development Finance Authority postponed Wednesday final action on a bond program involving Allstate Insurance Co, a unit of AllState Corp, until its January board meeting.

Under the innovative program, Allstate would participate in a public/private relationship allowing it to purchase bonds of social service agencies in Illinois with limited credit enhancement provided by the authority.
However, some authority board members expressed concern about how the credit enhancement would work.

Stephen Welcome, the authority's general counsel, said that at issue is how the authority's credit enhancement funds would be applied to the transactions -- either on an aggregate basis or a per deal basis.
Bobby Wilkerson, the authority's director, said there were also discrepancies between the levels of credit enhancement acceptable to the authority, Gov. Jim Edgar's office and Allstate.
He explained that Allstate wants the authority to provide a 10 percent reserve for each deal, while the governor's office has set the level at seven percent and the authority at eight percent.
Wilkerson said the board wants him to get together with the company and the governor's office to reconcile the percentages.
As conceived, the program would provide up to $50 million of financing for social service agencies largely dependent on state contracts for their funding.

Wilkerson said the authority has $12 million to $13 million of credit enhancement funds available. So far, only two deals have been identified, $15 million of bonds for a group of agencies on Chicago's southside called CARES, and $5 million for Decatur Mental Health Center, according to Wilkerson.

Another problem is how long the authority's credit enhancement would stay in place. Wilkerson said Allstate wants the authority's funds to stay in the deals for 10 years, while the authority wants the option to be bought out of the deals by the social service agencies before that time.
An Allstate official has said the authority's role in structuring the deals and providing credit enhancement were key to the company's interest in the program.
The aim of the program is to give social service providers access to the debt market at lower costs by eliminating the need for a letter of credit or bond insurance.
Wilkerson said that he has received some preliminary interest in the program from other institutional buyers, adding it was too premature to talk about their possible participation.
